Today marks the 12th anniversary of a vision rooted in the simple belief that "India can manufacture for the world". 🇮🇳

Looking back on 2014, one may recall debates about India's manufacturing potential. At a time when many products used in India were imported, PM Narendra Modi ji refused to accept that as our fate.

He envisioned an India that would not only manufacture for its own needs but would also create products for the world. An India where products used across the globe would proudly carry the tag 'Made in India' and be known for their quality.

We are witnessing that vision taking shape.

The numbers tell an encouraging story. India recorded its highest-ever annual FDI inflow of USD 94.53 billion in FY 2025-26, while cumulative FDI inflows from FY 2014-15 to FY 2025-26 reached USD 843 billion.

Greenfield industrial smart cities are being set up across the country under the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme to build infrastructure for globally competitive manufacturing.

Ease of Doing Business reforms have simplified regulations and reduced the compliance burden, while reforms in key sectors have created new opportunities for investment and manufacturing.

The PLI schemes have added further momentum. As of March 31, 2026, they have resulted in ₹2.40 lakh crore of actual investment, ₹23.8 lakh crore in production/sales and ₹15.2 lakh crore in exports, while generating over 14.6 lakh direct & indirect jobs.

Sectors such as electronics and telecom, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, automobiles, IT hardware, and speciality steel have significantly benefited from the PLI schemes.

The Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) is giving a huge boost to small enterprises, and over 470 crore orders have been placed through the platform.

But the real story of Make in India goes beyond these numbers.

It is the confidence it has created. The confidence among our startup founders, entrepreneurs, manufacturers, innovators, exporters and, most importantly, our people that ‘India can make, India can innovate, and India can compete with the world’.

#12YearsOfMakeInIndia is therefore not just a milestone. It reminds us what can happen when a nation believes in its own capabilities and the government powers that belief with sustained reforms and action.

The journey of Make in India continues, with an even bigger ambition: making India a global manufacturing powerhouse, which will also strengthen our Viksit Bharat by 2047 vision.

We hosted a 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗶𝗼-𝗔𝗜: 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆-𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, in collaboration with Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) Hyderabad, the Institute of genomics and integrative biology (CSIR) and the BRIC - Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD).

Dr. Satya Prakash Dash, Prof. Ullas Kolthur and Dr. Anand Anandkumar initiated the session. This was followed by speakers from academia, startups and industry sharing their expertise, with the aim of identifying, generating and building real collaborations and partnerships that are problem specific.

The discussion highlighted the need for good-quality datasets that are specific to our population and geography; compute that is still too slow for the work being asked of it; and the design-build-test-learn cycle — keeping the lab inside the loop, so that every computational prediction meets an experiment and every experimental result improves the next model. Alongside this came the harder question of validation, and what metrics we should be using to build and judge these algorithms in the first place.

The emphasis was on building shared, open capability rather than parallel private efforts.

Our thanks to every speaker and participant for their time and open conversation.

Somethings are best kept cool. Fresh produce is definitely one of them.

But keeping things cool while they’re on the move? That’s where it gets tricky.

Meet Tan90 Thermal, a Chennai-based social innovation start-up asking a simple question: can we keep things cold without ice, electricity and bulky machinery?

India’s cold-chain infrastructure faces a persistent gap. Limited capacity, high operating cost of reefer trucks and inefficient last-mile logistics lead to significant wastage of perishables. At the same time, the sector’s dependence on fossil fuels adds on to the financial and environmental burden.

These are the problems Tan90 set out to solve. Using phase change materials, they have created portable storage units that keep products cold without the need for continuous refrigeration or electricity.

Today, their Cooling-as-a-Service model helps food, pharmaceuticals, modern retail and other sectors keep things cool when quality and cost are on the line. And they have been at it for 7 years, across 4+ countries, supporting 500+ businesses and deploying 5 lakh+ units.

But there is a lot more to their journey.

Are ceramics truly sustainable just because they come from earth?

In this month’s Founder Insight Series, we spotlight Mr Shashank Nimkar, Founder of Earth Tatva - Recycled Ceramics, a startup rethinking ceramic waste through circular material innovation.

While ceramics are often seen as natural and eco-friendly, fired clay does not biodegrade easily and continues to accumulate in landfills for generations. From discarded kulhads to industrial ceramic rejects, the waste problem is much larger than we often imagine.

Through TatvaMix, Earth Tatva is working to recycle landfilled ceramic waste back into mouldable clay, helping reduce the mining of natural resources and enabling existing ceramic manufacturers to move towards a closed-loop production process.

Read the full article to understand why sustainability must go beyond perception and why the future of ceramics needs to be circular by design.

B2B or B2C? Your customer decides how you should go to market. 👇

A strong product is only one part of the equation. Your Go-To-Market (GTM) strategy needs to change based on who you're selling to.

In B2B, buying decisions often involve multiple stakeholders, longer evaluation cycles, business value, reliability, and measurable results.

In B2C, the journey is often more direct, with factors such as price, convenience, brand, experience, and customer preference playing a major role.

For startups, understanding this difference can help you make better decisions around:

🔹 Who your real decision-maker is
🔹 What motivates your customer to buy
🔹 Where you should reach them
🔹 How your sales journey should work
🔹 Which metrics actually matter
